title: Cherry Pickup II
statement:
A farm is laid out as a grid with `r` rows and `c` columns. Cell `(i, j)` holds `grid[i][j]` cherries.

Two robots collect cherries. Robot A starts at the top-left cell `(0, 0)` and robot B starts at the top-right cell `(0, c - 1)`. Both robots move at the same time, one row down per step, until they reach the last row. When a robot is at cell `(i, j)` it moves to one of `(i + 1, j - 1)`, `(i + 1, j)` or `(i + 1, j + 1)`, and it may never leave the grid.

Whenever a robot stands on a cell it picks all the cherries there and the cell becomes empty. If both robots stand on the same cell at the same time, the cherries of that cell are counted only once. The two robots are allowed to cross each other.

Find the maximum total number of cherries the two robots can collect together.
inputFormat:
The first line contains `r` and `c`.
Each of the next `r` lines contains `c` integers: the cherries in that row.
outputFormat: Print a single integer: the maximum total number of cherries.

examples.explanation: Robot A walks (0,0), (1,0), (2,1) and collects 3 + 2 + 5 = 10. Robot B walks (0,2), (1,1), (2,2) and collects 1 + 5 + 5 = 11. They never share a cell, so the total is 21, and no pair of paths does better.
A starts on 4 and B on 7. Row 1 has 6 and 9: A moves to column 0 (6) and B to column 1 (9). Total 4 + 7 + 6 + 9 = 26.
With a single column both robots always share a cell, so each cell is counted once: 5 + 8 = 13.

hints: Think of the two robots as one combined state. Because they move row by row in lock-step, the state is just the row and both columns.
Define `dp[row][a][b]` as the best total when robot A is in column `a` and robot B in column `b` on this row. Each state has up to 3 x 3 predecessors.
Only the previous row is needed, so keep two `c x c` tables. Remember to add the cell value only once when `a == b`.
